task.title: Style a drawing
task.shortdesc: You can style the elements of a drawing with attributes, with rules in the drawing and, when the drawing is part of your XML, with the style sheet of your document.

step.cmd: Use presentation attributes for simple drawings

info.p: Most properties of a drawing can be written as attributes of the element, such as fill, stroke, stroke-width and font-size. These are presentation attributes. A presentation attribute is the weakest style an element can have: any rule overrides it.

step.cmd: Use rules for the styles you repeat

info.p: A drawing follows the rules of CSS: selectors, specificity, inheritance and the order of the cascade. These sources of style can reach an element:

ul.li: The presentation attributes of the element. They are the weakest.
The rules of the style sheet of your document, when the drawing is part of your XML.
The rules in a style element inside the drawing. They come after the rules of your document.
The style attribute of the element. It wins over the rules.

info.p: The rules follow the usual order: the more specific selector wins, and the later rule wins when the specificity is the same. A declaration marked !important wins over the rest.

stepxmp.pre: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="60"> <style> .warning { fill: #f2d4d4; stroke: #8a2a2a; } </style> <rect class="warning" width="100" height="60"/> </svg>

info.p: A type selector without a namespace matches the elements of any namespace. When your XML has elements named like those of SVG, such as text, use a namespace in the selector:

The properties of paint and text are inherited. Set fill or stroke on a g element and every shape inside it uses them. A drawing in your XML also inherits the properties of the elements around it, such as font-family and color. The keyword currentColor is the value of color, so a drawing can follow the color of the text:

stepxmp.pre: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="16" height="16"> <circle cx="8" cy="8" r="7" fill="currentColor"/> </svg>

info.p: Custom properties work too: define --accent on the svg element and write fill: var(--accent) in a rule.

The geometry of the shapes is also a set of CSS properties: x, y, width and height for rectangles, cx, cy and r for circles, rx and ry for ellipses and rounded corners, and d for the data of a path. A rule that sets them has the same effect as the attributes, and it can use any length unit and calc():
Percentages refer to the size of the drawing, or to the area of its viewBox when it has one.

step.cmd: Choose the fonts of the text

info.p: The text of a drawing in your XML uses the fonts of your document, including the fonts that its @font-face rules define. A style element in the drawing can define more fonts for that drawing. A drawing in a file does not see the fonts of your document: it uses the standard fonts, the fonts you give to CSSMedia with the option -f, and its own @font-face rules.
